what_it_does: Complementary FET (CFET) is a next-generation transistor design that stacks the two flavors of transistor — p-type (PMOS) and n-type (NMOS) — directly on top of each other instead of placing them side-by-side, shrinking the chip footprint significantly. This vertical stacking, however, makes wiring the transistors together much harder because there are fewer tracks on the visible top surface. This paper tackles that problem by also routing metal wires on the back side of the chip wafer, a relatively new technique called backside metal (BS) routing. The authors build an automated synthesis flow — the process that translates a logical circuit description into a physical transistor layout — that plans both front and back wiring together, and also handles folding transistors so they fit in tighter spaces. They use mathematical tools including Euler path analysis (finding efficient routes through graphs) and satisfiability modulo theories (SMT, a solver that figures out whether a set of constraints can all be satisfied at once) to place devices and route wires optimally. This is based on the abstract alone, so exact area or speed results are not confirmed.
